channel.title: TEST Plainly Put
channel.description: One topic per episode, anything from bridge engineering to sleep, explained plainly in about twenty-five minutes. Claude researches and writes each episode from a handful of sources, all listed in the show notes, and a synthetic voice reads it. Where the evidence is thin, the episode says so.

item.title: TEST Episode 3: Serotonin and your gut
item.description:
Higher-risk topic: discusses antidepressants and other prescription drugs, and irritable bowel syndrome.

More than 90% of the body's serotonin is made in the gut, not the brain, and it cannot cross the blood-brain barrier. Gut serotonin moves food along, signals fullness and nausea to the brainstem, and is carried in platelets, which hold over 95% of the serotonin in the blood and use it in clotting.

In mice, gut bacteria, especially spore-forming species, prompt the gut's own cells to make serotonin: the microbiota accounted for 64% of colonic and 49% of blood serotonin, while bacteria made under 10% directly. These results are in mice and cell models, not yet in people.

The gut talks to the brain along the vagus nerve. A Lactobacillus rhamnosus strain that reduced anxiety-like behaviour in mice, an effect that vanished when the vagus nerve was cut, had no effect over placebo on mood, stress, sleep or cognition in 29 healthy men over 8 weeks.

Drugs acting on gut serotonin have the firmest evidence: 5-HT3 blockers such as ondansetron for chemotherapy nausea, and antidepressants for irritable bowel syndrome. A 2025 meta-analysis of 28 trials (2,475 patients) found tricyclics cut the risk of global symptoms persisting (RR 0.70, moderate certainty), and SSRIs helped abdominal pain (RR 0.74, 7 trials, low certainty). SSRIs can also cause gut side effects, speeding transit or causing constipation. If you take an antidepressant, talk to your prescriber before changing it.

Sources

Gut microbes promote colonic serotonin production through an effect of short-chain fatty acids on enterochromaffin cells. FASEB J 29(4):1395-1403. https://doi.org/10.1096/fj.14-259598.
